name: Dark Olive
lede: Dark Olive is a dim, grey-brown olive that sits between green and brown, and it is one of the most common dark colors in the paintings of our archive.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The swatch carries a Ridgway plate number from 1912 and a block in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, and it matches the German standard color RAL 7013, which is sold as brown grey [1]. Its older shades include names such as Pullman Green and Crystal Palace Green, the latter recorded by about 1904 [1]. The xkcd survey of 2010 added the plain phrase Dark Olive [1].

Books use the words as a plain description, not a pigment name. Paterson's dictionary defines ivy green simply as a dark olive green [2]. St Clair's color glossary defines olive drab as green with plenty of gray and brown, a dull olive, which is close to this swatch [4]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[umber]] and [[olive]], and it sits near [[moss]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive a color near this swatch appears in 2,656 of 23,781 paintings, or 11.2 per cent, which is more common than 94 per cent of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1800s, at 8.3 per cent of that century's paintings, and in a painting it most often plays a hidden color [3]. Willem Roelofs has it in 6 of his 12 works here, 4.1 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].
